article.title: Slip and Fall Claims
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. After a fall, many people feel embarrassed and want to leave quickly. That reaction is understandable. But leaving without reporting what happened can make your claim harder to prove later. An incident report creates an early written record of the fall. It can show where the accident happened, when it happened, who was present, and what condition may have caused it. If the property owner later denies the incident or disputes the details, that report may become important. If you search “ slip and fall attorney near me ” and reach out to the right expert, they can review the report and compare it with photos, witness statements, medical records, and other evidence. What Is an Incident Report? An incident report is a document created after an accident occurs on someone else’s property. It may be completed by a store manager, restaurant employee, apartment manager, hotel staff member, security officer, or property owner. The report usually includes basic facts, such as: Date and time of the fall Exact location Description of what happened Names of employees involved Witness names Hazard description Initial injury complaints Actions taken after the fall The report does not decide the claim by itself. It is a starting point. It helps create a timeline that can later be checked against other evidence. Why Quick Reporting Matters Time matters after a slip and fall. A spill may be cleaned within minutes. A loose mat may be moved. A broken item may be repaired. Surveillance footage may be overwritten. Reporting the fall quickly helps show that the incident happened at that location and on that date. It also makes it harder for a business or property owner to later say they had no record of the accident. Prompt reporting can also document the hazard before the scene changes. If you slipped on a wet floor, tripped over damaged flooring, or fell because of poor lighting, the report may identify the unsafe condition while details are still fresh. What the Report Should Include The report should be accurate and specific. You do not need to guess or fill in details you do not know. Important information may include: Where the fall happened What you saw on the floor or walkway What part of your body hurt Names of employees who responded Names and contact details of witnesses Whether photos or video may exist Whether medical help was requested Avoid saying you are “fine” if you are unsure. Pain can increase later. It is better to say what you feel at the time and seek medical care if symptoms continue. Incident Reports Can Help Show Notice Notice is a key issue in many slip and fall claims. In simple terms, notice means the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. Actual notice may exist if an employee saw the hazard before the fall or a customer reported it. Constructive notice may exist if the condition was present long enough that the property owner should have found it through reasonable care. For falls involving a transitory foreign substance in a business establishment, Florida Statute § 768.0755 requires the injured person to prove the business had actual or constructive knowledge of the dangerous condition and should have acted. An incident report may identify who responded, what hazard was reported, and what staff knew at the time. That information can help build the notice timeline. Reports Work Best With Other Evidence An incident report is useful, but it should not be the only proof. It works best when supported by other documentation. Helpful evidence may include: Photos of the hazard Surveillance footage Witness statements Maintenance records Cleaning logs Medical records Receipts showing you were present A Boynton Beach injury lawyer may compare the incident report with these records. If the report says the floor was dry, but photos show a puddle, that conflict matters. If the report omits a witness, that witness may still be important. The goal is to build a full record, not rely on one document. What If You Cannot Get a Copy? Some businesses may not give you a copy of the incident report right away. That does not mean you should skip the reporting step. Ask for a copy. If they refuse, write down who took the report, their job title, the date, and the time. Keep your own notes about what happened and what was said. You can also preserve your own evidence by taking photos, saving receipts, and collecting witness contact information. A copy of the report may be requested later through the claims process. Common Problems With Incident Reports Incident reports are not always complete. Some may be vague or written from the property owner’s perspective. Others may leave out key details. Common problems include: Wrong location Missing witness names No description of the hazard Incorrect time Limited injury description Statements you did not make Failure to mention photos or video If you notice an error, keep your own written notes. Do not sign anything that is inaccurate. If you are asked to sign, read it carefully first. Florida Fault Rules and Deadlines Florida’s modified comparative negligence rule can affect slip-and-fall claims. In covered negligence actions, a person found greater than 50 percent at fault for their own harm may not recover damages. This matters because a property owner may argue that you were not watching where you were walking. An incident report can help preserve facts before blame is shifted. Florida law also gives two years for actions founded on negligence. Even so, evidence may disappear much sooner. Early reporting helps preserve the facts while they are still available. What to Do After You Report the Fall After the report is made, take a few additional steps to protect your claim. You should: Seek medical care promptly Photograph the hazard and the surrounding area Save shoes and clothing Keep receipts and medical records Write down symptoms and conversations with staff Collect witness information Avoid detailed insurer statements before understanding your options These steps can help connect the report to the full claim. Conclusion An incident report can play an important role in a Boynton Beach slip and fall claim. It creates an early record of when and where the fall happened, who responded, and what hazard may have caused the injury. The report is strongest when supported by photos, medical records, witness statements, and maintenance evidence.
